mcqs.question: Why does a K-map use Gray code ordering for its row and column labels instead of plain binary counting order?
options: Gray code makes the map fit more cells per row
Gray code ensures any two physically adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable, which is what makes visual grouping meaningful
Gray code is required to represent don't-care values
Plain binary counting order is mathematically invalid for truth tables
mcqs.explanation: Gray code changes only one bit between consecutive values. In a K-map, this guarantees that adjacent cells (which is what you group visually) differ in exactly one input variable -- the entire basis of the grouping method.

mcqs.question: Which of these is a valid K-map group size?
mcqs.explanation: Valid K-map groups must be a power of two in size (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...). 3, 5, and 6 are not powers of two and cannot form a legal group.

mcqs.question: Why do EDA tools use Quine-McCluskey (or similar algorithms) instead of K-maps for real circuit minimization?
options: Quine-McCluskey produces less accurate results but runs faster
K-maps are only visual/manual and become impractical beyond about 4-6 variables, while Quine-McCluskey scales algorithmically to any number of variables
K-maps cannot handle don't-care conditions at all
Quine-McCluskey is a hardware-only technique, not applicable in software
mcqs.explanation: K-maps rely on humans visually recognizing adjacency patterns, which stops being practical past roughly 4-6 variables. Quine-McCluskey replaces visual grouping with systematic tabular comparison, so it scales to circuits with dozens of variables.

mcqs.question: What K-map grouping mistake does a beginner make by only considering cells that look adjacent on the flat printed page?
options: They miss legal groups that wrap around from one edge of the map to the opposite edge
They form groups that are too large to be valid
They accidentally include don't-care cells that shouldn't be grouped
mcqs.explanation: K-map edges wrap around (the map is conceptually a torus, following the cyclic Gray-code labeling), so the leftmost and rightmost columns (and top/bottom rows) are adjacent. Missing this leads to a larger, non-minimal expression than necessary.
